summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, regardless of the gender of the participants, whether the act is consensual, or whether it takes place in private. Section 377D adds an undefined "gross indecency" offence carrying up to two years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, are usable against transgender people, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so they reach foreign visitors in Selangor.

Selangor maintains a state Sharia layer above the federal code. Its enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females" alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These state offences bind Muslims only; non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone. Enforcement is carried out by the state religious department, and the enactments contain no legal definition of transgender dress, so the line between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground rather than by any published standard.

Custodial punishment for same-sex conduct has in fact been imposed by a Selangor Syariah court: five men received six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. The same enactments permit non-custodial disposal, allowing sharia courts to commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and to order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states. At least 1,733 people had attended state rehabilitation programmes as of June 2021, under a crackdown on LGBT people that has run since the 2018 general election.

The Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 in February 2021 because the state legislature had exceeded its powers. The ruling turned on which legislature may enact the offence, not on the substance of the prohibition, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised as a result.

Violence against transgender women in Malaysia is lethal and largely unpunished, and Selangor is no exception: a trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months. Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, so there is no statutory remedy attached to that violence.

There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. The nearest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable throughout Malaysia, and Mahathir stated in June 2019 that the country cannot accept same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
Selangor's cross-dressing provisions are one data point in a national pattern. All 13 states, together with the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, maintain Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or a man posing as a woman, alongside liwat and musahaqah, and state Islamic religious departments carry out the enforcement. The Federal Court applied the same federalism reasoning to 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, leaving the national Penal Code framework intact in every case.

Investigations into LGBT people documented in August 2022 by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, indicating that surveillance and enforcement are operated as a multi-state effort rather than a local initiative. The same report found that state rehabilitation programmes internalise discrimination and foster self-hatred among participants.

Enforcement against social venues has escalated nationally since 2018. Police raided a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and 11 shopping malls in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches; on 28 November 2025 a raid on a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur produced 208 arrests under section 377B, with detainees' faces and personal details published after media were pre-tipped. A magistrate found no case made out under 377B when asked to extend remand, yet more than 130 detainees were still being held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Within days of the Home Minister saying on 2 December 2025 that the provisions would be revisited, police raided another sauna in Penang.

Official hostility has been stated at the highest levels. In July 2020 the Federal Territories Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, and the International Commission of Jurists demanded that the order be revoked.
localsOnly:
In 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear before a Selangor court to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest, announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, and then sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters cited the deployment as evidence of how far authorities will go to enforce rigid gender norms.

State religious enforcement is applied to Muslims resident in Selangor through the Syariah courts, which have jurisdiction over cross-dressing, liwat and musahaqah offences and can impose imprisonment, fines, caning, approved-home committal and institutional counselling or rehabilitation. Arrest of transgender people by religious officials is documented over decades, including repeated arrests of the same women more than twenty times, a mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding in June 2014, and a pattern of strip-searches and sexual assault during detention.

Identity documents remain under state control through the national Registration Department, which routinely rejects gender-marker changes. A 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict holds that sex is determined at birth and is unaffected by reassignment surgery; it was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the Registration Department to update a trans man's identity card, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.

The 1,733 recorded participants in state rehabilitation programmes as of June 2021 are drawn from the national crackdown that has run since the 2018 general election. No political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime statute protects residents on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.
